provenance.source_title: The water footprint of artificial intelligence: Emerging solutions and governance imperatives

content.reading_plan: This is a Water Research “Making Waves” review and policy argument, combining technical definitions, reported quantitative estimates, facility examples, and normative recommendations. It is moderately dense, with especially concentrated material in the accounting definitions and technology comparisons. I will follow its sections in order, usually taking a few paragraphs or one technical subsection per step, separating reported evidence from interpretation and recommendations. The prepared text splits the methodological opening across sections; I read those fragments together as the description of the review method. Table 1 is read with its footnotes and retained image.

reading_path.moves: Opening problem framing, quantitative forecast, scope statement, and announcement of a governance framework.

claims.text: AI's environmental footprint is still assessed mainly through electricity consumption and greenhouse-gas emissions, while freshwater consumption is a less visible dimension.
AI infrastructure consumes freshwater through evaporative cooling, electricity generation, and semiconductor manufacturing.
AI's global water footprint could reach 4.2–6.6 billion cubic meters annually by 2027.
Two-thirds of post-2022 data centers are located in water-stressed regions.
Technologies can reduce on-site water demand, but deployment remains limited by policy gaps.

Digital water sobriety links evaluation of which AI uses justify freshwater consumption, water-conscious siting, and mandatory facility-level transparency; water-sustainable AI requires fundamental policy reform, not merely technological optimization.

reading_path.meaning: The opening establishes an explicitly governance-oriented perspective: water is presented not just as an engineering input but as a constraint on the justification and location of computing. These are introductory assertions and forecasts whose grounds have not yet unfolded.

reading_path.moves: Contrast between user experience and physical infrastructure; quantitative illustration; classification and scope restriction.

claims.text: AI appears intangible and effectively costless to users, yet conversations, image generation, and training produce waste heat that often requires water-intensive cooling.
AI-related water consumption is substantial.

support.text: The cited analysis estimates approximately 700,000 liters of clean freshwater for training GPT-3 and a 500 ml bottle equivalent for 10–50 medium-length responses.

Hyperscale AI facilities amplify localized water stress by concentrating demand at individual sites.

support.text: Rack power densities of 50–100+ kW are contrasted with 5–10 kW in conventional enterprise facilities; one hyperscale training site can concentrate the water demand of dozens of smaller centers.

claims.text: These distinctions establish that AI infrastructure presents a qualitatively different water challenge from general-purpose cloud computing, warranting dedicated assessment and mitigation strategies.

reading_path.meaning: The argument moves from showing that computing uses water to explaining why AI deserves distinct treatment. Continuous utilization and site-level concentration supplement the simpler claim that more computation produces more heat.

reading_path.location: Section 2, including its displaced methodological opening
reading_path.moves: Method description, conceptual definitions, reporting qualification, and statement of exclusions.

claims.text: The targeted review synthesizes peer-reviewed studies identified through Web of Science and Google Scholar for 2015–2025, corporate reports and technical documentation, and investigative journalism and policy analyses; peer-reviewed sources were prioritized.

Water footprint is a broad freshwater-appropriation framework formally standardized in ISO 14046, distinguishing blue surface and groundwater consumption, green soil-stored rainwater, and grey water required to assimilate pollutants.

support.text: The author draws on water-footprint and LCA literature to introduce these categories.

support.text: The distinction is grounded in freshwater LCA literature and illustrated with research on thermal pollution from power plants.

claims.text: Although the review focuses on operational blue water consumption measured through WUE, most cited figures represent withdrawals unless otherwise specified because reporting often conflates withdrawal and consumption.
The review makes no independent footprint calculation; comprehensive green, grey, scarcity-weighted, electricity-related, and semiconductor-related assessment lies outside its scope.

reading_path.meaning: This section adds an essential interpretive caution to the preceding large numbers: the intended object is consumption, but much of the available evidence measures withdrawal. The review presents itself as synthesis rather than a new calculation, while defining dimensions its operational focus leaves out.

reading_path.moves: Metric definition and tabular comparison, with estimation and system-boundary qualifications.

claims.text: WUE divides annual site water used for cooling and humidification by annual IT energy consumption, expressed in liters/kWh or m³/MWh.

support.text: The definition is attributed to an explanation of data center WUE.

citations.reference_entry: Higgins, A., 2024. What is water usage effectiveness (WUE) in data centers? https://blog. equinix.com/blog/2024/11/13/what-is-water-usage-effectiveness-wue-in-data-c enters/(accessed 05.12.25).

claims.text: Table 1 (gap T1) compares typical WUE in L/kWh separately from representative annual consumption in m³ per 1 MW of IT capacity. Evaporative cooling is listed at 2.0–3.0+ and about 25,500; cold-climate free-air cooling at below 0.3 and below 1,000; natural-water-body cooling at below 0.2 and approximately zero; subsea at zero for both; waterless systems at approximately zero on-site; and reclaimed-water systems at variable WUE with evaporative-like volumes but non-potable supply.

support.text: The table pairs evaporative cooling's high water use with high energy efficiency, free-air cooling with geographic and seasonal limits, natural-water cooling with 5–8°C thermal discharge, subsea cooling with capital costs and ecological unknowns, waterless cooling with electricity penalties and hot-climate degradation, and reclaimed water with dual infrastructure and regional availability constraints.

claims.text: The free-air estimates are approximate because Meta Luleå's IT capacity is not public; low natural-water-body consumption does not eliminate thermal pollution; and waterless on-site operation may shift consumption to power generation.

support.text: Table 1's footnotes identify a reported Luleå withdrawal of 25,400 m³/year, water returned to source in closed-loop systems, and the dependence of indirect consumption on grid mix.

claims.text: Fully air-cooled facilities approach zero WUE, whereas heavily evaporative facilities may exceed three m³/MWh depending on climate and system design.

support.text: The author cites the U.S. data center energy report for this range.

claims.text: Microsoft's 2024 discontinuation of the technically successful 2018–2020 Project Natick demonstration suggests economic or operational constraints.

Potential subsea effects include thermal and acoustic disturbance, electromagnetic emissions, chemical leaching, and benthic disruption. Initial assessments report temperature rises below 1°C, but comprehensive ecological monitoring remains unpublished.
High capital costs, complex maintenance, limited suitable sites, and underdeveloped regulation constrain subsea scaling.

reading_path.meaning: Subsea cooling sharpens the distinction between eliminating freshwater use and establishing an environmentally and operationally satisfactory system. The author explicitly marks the inference from Natick's termination as suggestive rather than definitive.

reading_path.moves: Synthesis of trade-offs, emerging-technology qualification, and transition from engineering to governance.

claims.text: Three linked tensions constrain deployment: financial incentives favor cheap water-intensive cooling; dry cooling trades water savings for electricity and carbon costs; and sunny low-carbon-power regions tend to be arid, whereas northern free-air sites have limited solar resources and hydropower water costs.

support.text: The regional comparison again invokes reservoir evaporation in hydropower.

citations.reference_entry: Scherer, L., Pfister, S., 2016. Global water footprint assessment of hydropower. Renew. Energy. 99, 711–720.

claims.text: No single siting or technology choice resolves all three tensions simultaneously, underscoring the need for integrated assessment across water, energy, and carbon dimensions.

Technology companies are exploring dedicated nuclear supply, including SMRs; this could reduce water associated with fossil-grid electricity, but conventionally cooled reactors may shift rather than eliminate demand, with net effects depending on design and siting.
Technology alone is insufficient; water-sustainable AI requires governance establishing accountability, standardized disclosure, and reframed expectations about digital resource consumption.

reading_path.meaning: The repeated technology trade-offs are consolidated into an argument for integrated assessment and governance. The transition builds on the adoption and scaling constraints already identified, rather than treating engineering feasibility as equivalent to implementation.

reading_path.moves: Framework definition, market-failure explanation, value distinctions, and proposed governance mechanisms.

claims.text: Digital water sobriety challenges unconstrained AI expansion through three dimensions: judging applications' water costs, water-conscious siting, and mandatory facility-level transparency.

support.text: The author reports that 73% of UK respondents were unfamiliar with digital pollution as evidence that evaluation is urgent.

citations.reference_entry: Tsoury, A., Barnett-Itzhaki, Z., 2025. Exploring the associations between socioeconomic and demographic factors and literacy in environmental and digital pollution. Sustainability 17 (14), 6336.

claims.text: Concentration in stressed regions reflects market failure: electricity costs, latency, tax incentives, and land drive siting, while bulk-priced water fails to register scarcity and opportunity costs. Companies consequently externalize costs onto communities and ecosystems, a pattern that will persist without regulation.

Medical diagnostics, climate modeling, and pharmaceutical discovery may justify significant water expenditure even in constrained regions; recreational image generation, automated marketing, and low-stakes queries have more diffuse value that is difficult to justify against domestic and agricultural needs in stressed watersheds.
The framework advocates graduated governance rather than binary application approval or prohibition, linking resource expenditure to demonstrated societal benefit.

Practical mechanisms could include scarcity-adjusted prices, water-impact assessments above computational thresholds, real-time watershed-linked facility budgets, and preferential permits for water-efficient cooling.

reading_path.meaning: The earlier contrast between essential and discretionary uses becomes an explicit normative spectrum. The author qualifies it by rejecting a simple ban/approval division and proposes pricing, assessment, and permitting instruments instead.

reading_path.location: Section 5.1, implementation cautions and closing paragraphs
reading_path.moves: Concession through governance analogies, qualified institutional optimism, behavioral evidence, and foundational value premise.

claims.text: Climate and biodiversity governance warn of free-riding, jurisdictional fragmentation, and industry resistance; water may offer advantages because impacts are local and visible and allocation rights, permits, and municipal authority already exist.
Effective digital water sobriety requires sustained political will and enforceable regulation, not merely voluntary commitments.
Awareness alone is insufficient; structural policy and education must be integrated.

support.text: Studies report weak correlations between knowledge of digital pollution and willingness to adopt sustainable practices.

citations.reference_entry: Barnett-Itzhaki, Z., Tsoury, A., 2025. From awareness to action: a UK-based study on public perceptions of digital pollution. Sustainability 17 (17), 7839.

claims.text: Freshwater is a finite common resource requiring equitable allocation; AI's footprint results from deliberate policy and design choices rather than technological necessity, requiring coordinated regulatory, educational, and industrial action.

reading_path.meaning: The framework is not presented as self-executing. The author tempers institutional optimism with implementation obstacles and distinguishes public knowledge from behavioral change, while making the common-resource value premise explicit.

reading_path.moves: Assessment of voluntary commitments, explanation of accountability gaps, early regulatory examples, and transparency recommendations.

claims.text: Corporate responses remain inadequate: replenishment pledges do not resolve temporal and spatial mismatches between continuous localized consumption and seasonal distributed replenishment.

support.text: Google and Microsoft are reported to have pledged water positivity by 2030, replenishing more water than they consume in stressed regions through credits, restoration, or infrastructure investment.

citations.reference_entry: Paresh D., 2021. Google to replenish 20% more water than it uses by 2030. https://www. reuters.com/business/sustainable-business/google-replenish-20-more-water-than-ituses-by-2030-2021-09-09/(Accessed 29.11.25).

claims.text: Voluntary, unstandardized WUE reporting and corporate aggregation obscure local impacts and prevent meaningful site comparison.
Regulation is beginning to address consumption but transparency remains severely limited.

support.text: Virginia's proposed bill would mandate annual reporting from major facilities; the author also reports emerging initiatives in Europe and the western United States.

citations.reference_entry: Barratt, L., Gambarini, C., Uteuova, A., 2025. Revealed: big tech’s new datacentres will take water from the world’s driest areas. https://www.theguardian.com/environme nt/2025/apr/09/big-tech-datacentres-water (accessed 15.11.25).

claims.text: Operators' commercial-sensitivity claims prevent reliable footprint assessment; standardized mandatory disclosure must cover locations, cooling configurations, and electricity sources.

support.text: The passage cites Jain when describing missing or aggregated information needed for comprehensive understanding.

citations.reference_entry: Jain, P., 2025. From bottleneck to breakthrough: AI in chip verification: how AI is transforming chip design with smarter verification methods. https://spectrum.ieee. org/calibre-vision-ai-chip-design (accessed 05.12.25).

reading_path.meaning: The author applies the framework to existing corporate and regulatory practices. Repeated Microsoft and Google percentages serve as reminders rather than new evidence; the new emphasis is on why replenishment and aggregation cannot substitute for local, temporally specific accountability.

reading_path.moves: Restatement of feasibility and structured research agenda.

claims.text: Facility-level accounting does not attribute water costs to specific models, training runs, or architectures; workload-to-water benchmark datasets across cooling configurations would support optimization and application-level judgments.

Electricity- and semiconductor-embedded water remain poorly quantified, especially during renewable transitions; integrated lifecycle assessment should include regional generation's spatial and temporal variation.

support.text: Agricultural assessment is offered as an example of spatially and temporally explicit water accounting.

citations.reference_entry:
Pfister, S., Bayer, P., 2014. Monthly water stress: spatially and temporally explicit

- consumptive water footprint of global crop production. J. Clean Prod. 73, 52–62.

claims.text: Ecological monitoring of lakeside and subsea cooling remains a research priority.
Cross-city evidence on district-heating costs, legacy-network integration, and operation under different conditions remains limited despite pilot viability.
Standardized protocols specifying measurement methods, temporal resolution, and geographic granularity are foundational for facility comparison, watershed assessment, and effective governance.

reading_path.meaning: Previously identified limitations become a research program. The author returns to the lifecycle boundary set in Section 2 and to the ecological and heat-recovery uncertainties of Section 4, while adding the need to connect facility totals to particular AI workloads.

reading_path.moves: Policy synthesis and concrete recommendations, partly restating earlier proposals.

claims.text: Mandatory facility-level reporting should extend WUE disclosure to on-site consumption, electricity-embedded water, and temporal variation.

New construction should be restricted in severely stressed watersheds, with cumulative impact assessment required in water concessions and permitting to prevent costs being externalized onto vulnerable communities.
Tiered governance should link deployment to demonstrated societal benefit and local availability rather than computational economics alone.

Policies favoring district-heating integration over simple direct cooling would accelerate solutions that displace fossil thermal generation and associated water use, producing energy, climate, and water co-benefits.

reading_path.meaning: The research agenda is followed by an implementation agenda. Scarcity pricing, training assessments, budgets, and preferential permitting are restated rather than newly introduced; the explicit restriction on construction and expanded disclosure requirements give the recommendations sharper operational form.

reading_path.moves: Resource-justice conclusion, reprise of contrasting cases, assignment of responsibility, and conditional warning.

claims.text: As AI expands, the central question shifts from marginal efficiency to resource justice: how much "intelligence" per liter of water is justified as both energy and freshwater become constrained?
Computational infrastructure consuming public water during drought while agricultural communities face restrictions represents governance failure, not technical constraint.

support.text: The conclusion contrasts the previously discussed Luleå and zero-freshwater subsea examples with Colon, interpreting their differences as consequences of policy and siting choices.

claims.text: Decisions about deployment, cooling, and whose water is consumed will determine whether AI worsens vulnerable populations' insecurity or catalyzes integrated water-energy-heat innovation.

Water-sustainable AI is achievable, but whether political will, accountability, and public awareness develop quickly enough will determine whether expansion irreversibly deepens stress in vulnerable regions.

reading_path.meaning: The conclusion does not add a new technological pathway; it uses earlier contrasts to relocate the final question from efficiency to distributive choice and political will. The warning preserves the author's strong urgency while remaining framed around decisions still to be made.

reading_path.meaning: The article closes with administrative declarations and its reference list rather than further argument. The no-data declaration sits alongside the earlier description of a literature and disclosure synthesis, not an independent footprint calculation. The references document the mixed scholarly, corporate, journalistic, and policy source base; their contents have not been independently checked here.
